routes.description: Establish Christian theism as more plausible than skeptical agnosticism through a cumulative case from cosmic fine-tuning and origin, objective morality, the resurrection and Christian revelation, and experiences of numinous beauty, while accounting for evolutionary suffering and the absence of coercive proof.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the converging considerations are reasonably explained by a loving, orderly creator and specifically support Christian commitment, with the evidential force of the whole exceeding the skeptical alternatives and the counterevidence from suffering and uncertainty.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined evidence makes Christian theism more plausible than skeptical agnosticism.

centralBridges.description: Connect cosmic existence and life-permitting physical constants to an intelligent, orderly creator rather than an unexplained or multiverse alternative.
Connect historical resurrection claims and revelation to Christianity rather than merely generic creator theism.
Show that morality and beauty reinforce the scientific and historical considerations as a cumulative case despite uncertainty.
Explain why evolutionary and physical suffering remain compatible with a loving God who creates through stable natural laws.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend rational commitment on substantial but noncoercive evidence rather than requiring mathematical proof.
Explain how divine purposes may operate through physical, evolutionary, and neural mechanisms without competing with them.

routes.description: Establish skeptical agnosticism as the more warranted position by showing that the concept of God and the proposed evidence underdetermine Christian theism, that fine-tuning admits reversal or alternatives, that resurrection and public-revelation claims lack sufficient historical support, and that extensive suffering weighs against a loving creator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the named considerations remain mysteries or support multiple explanations rather than preferentially supporting Christianity, especially when the improbability of apparently avoidable suffering under loving-creator theism is included in the comparative assessment.

motionBridge.description: Show that the total evidence does not warrant preferring Christian theism to skeptical agnosticism.

centralBridges.description: Show that disputed or incomprehensible divine attributes prevent the evidence from identifying the Christian God with adequate confidence.
Show that narrow physical constraints may be unexpected under omnipotent creation and do not uniquely favor a creator.
Show that extensive apparently avoidable evolutionary suffering is more expected under naturalism than under a loving creator.
Show that source-critical uncertainty and limits on private revelation weaken the move from generic possibility to Christianity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve naturalistic, evolutionary, legendary-development, and other rival explanations for the cited phenomena.
Distinguish acknowledging profound mysteries and existential stakes from claiming that they justify confident belief.

sections.title: Fine-tuning, cosmic explanation, and divine power
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal scientific case for an intelligent creator and the central skeptical challenge that physical fine-tuning may constrain or count against an omnipotent God, including multiverse and ultimate-explanation alternatives.

sections.title: Evolutionary suffering and orderly creation
sections.rationale: The comparative expectations of naturalism and loving-creator theism turn substantially on animal suffering, predation, extinction, and physical evil, together with the claim that stable natural laws and divine purposes explain their presence.

sections.title: Resurrection, Christian revelation, and historical warrant
sections.rationale: The resurrection and revelation are required to move the case from generic theism to Christianity, while Gospel source criticism, legendary development, martyrdom claims, Pauline testimony, and the public limits of private experience bear on that move.

sections.title: Morality, beauty, and transcendent experience
sections.rationale: Objective moral experience and numinous beauty provide distinct proposed signs of transcendence, while biblical moral concerns, aesthetic diversity, emotional and evolutionary accounts, and skeptical concessions define their comparative evidential reach.

sections.title: Cumulative evidence, uncertainty, and warranted commitment
sections.rationale: The debate ultimately compares a cumulative rationale for noncoercive Christian commitment with agnostic restraint toward several acknowledged mysteries, making standards of proof, conceptual clarity, combined evidential force, and existential significance burden-relevant.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Agnosticism is warranted because God's nonexistence cannot be established, while the observed world still supplies reasons to doubt a traditional creator.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly addresses Alex, and the uninterrupted first-person answer matches his stated agnostic position.

response.rationale: Constructively states the skeptical comparative posture: unresolved mysteries plus observed reasons for suspicion warrant agnostic restraint.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A clear constructive framing of the con route, though the cited span only compresses the specific reasons for doubting a traditional creator.

precisionFindings.rationale: The agnostic position and suspicion are recoverable, but the scope of the observed incompatibilities is not specified in this span.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The language of suspicion, betting, and agnosticism appropriately limits the conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move consistently distinguishes inability to disprove God from reasons to doubt a traditional creator, with the evidential bridge compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It invokes observation and mysteries but supplies few representative observations within the selected span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by stating why agnostic restraint is warranted.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing alternative is assessed in this framing move.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor explicitly identifies as agnostic, acknowledges mysteries, and says he is suspicious that the world is compatible with a traditional creator.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: God provides evidence sufficient for free personal commitment rather than coercive mathematical proof that would make belief unavoidable.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Collins to distinguish evidence from proof, and Collins answers by referring directly to his own book and theology.

response.rationale: Constructively supplies the epistemic standard under which evidence may rationally invite commitment without constituting unavoidable proof.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly establishes a supporting standard, though it does not yet demonstrate that the actual evidence meets it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidence-versus-proof distinction is stable; the sufficiency threshold for commitment remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Collins denies proof and advances a theological interpretation without presenting it as demonstrated fact.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Noncoercive evidence can coherently support voluntary trust, but the inference from divine intention to the absence of proof is underdefended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The central claim about God's intention is theological assertion rather than independently supported evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary epistemic-standard bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move sets Collins's standard without materially interpreting an opposing case.

moves.evidenceBasis: Collins expressly contrasts evidence for belief with proof and says incontrovertible proof would make acceptance unavoidable.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: The universe's beginning and fine-tuning, objective moral experience, beauty, and the failure of strict atheism jointly make trust in God reasonable.
moves.attributionBasis: Collins continues his answer without a speaker change, explicitly listing the considerations that moved him from atheism toward faith.

response.rationale: Constructively presents the listed scientific, moral, and aesthetic considerations as a cumulative reason to move from atheism and uncertainty toward trust.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It advances the overall route with multiple converging considerations, although their comparative combination is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative proposition is recoverable, but how much each consideration contributes and how independence is secured remain unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move describes reasonable trust after uncertainty rather than claiming deductive proof.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Convergence can rationally support trust, but the bridge from several suggestive considerations to God, and especially Christianity, is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several evidence categories are named, but their individual warrants, independence, and rival comparison are not developed here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly claims that the combined considerations make trust in God reasonable.

representationalCharity.rationale: No particular rival explanation is developed enough in this move to test charity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Collins lists cosmic beginning and fine-tuning, morality, and beauty, then explains that strict atheism had crumbled and trust became reasonable.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Christianity conflicts with the moral intuitions invoked as evidence for God because biblical treatments of slavery and women generate serious moral objections.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor continues uninterrupted, explicitly contrasts general agnosticism with his negative assessment of identifiable Christian traditions and texts.

components.text: Whether moral experience genuinely reinforces the cumulative case for Christian belief.
Whether the available evidence is sufficient for specifically Christian commitment.

response.rationale: O'Connor directly turns the invoked moral intuition against Christianity by citing biblical treatment of slavery and women, thereby contacting the moral component of Collins's cumulative case and the sufficiency of Christian evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive cumulative component but does not answer the scientific, aesthetic, or broader convergence claims.

precisionFindings.rationale: The internal moral-conflict objection is clear, though the exact passages and interpretive qualifications are omitted.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Serious moral qualms are supported as objections, but the broad conflict with Christianity depends on unpresented textual and interpretive detail.

charity.alternative: Christian moral reasoning may distinguish enduring moral principles from historically conditioned biblical practices.
charity.decisiveQualification: The selected span cites slavery and women without addressing that interpretive distinction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Using the same moral faculty both as evidence for God and as criticism of Christian sources is a coherent internal challenge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete topics are named, but no biblical text, interpretation, or representative comparison is supplied in the selected evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the central claim that morality reinforces the cumulative Christian case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection is live and relevant but omits a decisive source-supported qualification available to the opposing position.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor expressly says the moral intuition offered as evidence for God also produces objections concerning Christianity's treatment of slavery and women.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: Life-permitting physical constants require explanation, and an intelligent creator is more plausible than an empirically inaccessible multiverse while also addressing why anything exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator invites an explanation of fine-tuning, and Collins provides a sustained scientific and theological account through the next speaker transition.

response.rationale: Constructively connects life-permitting constants to a demand for explanation and compares an intelligent creator favorably with an empirically inaccessible multiverse.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely develops a central creator bridge with a specific explanandum and rival, though probability assumptions remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is clear, but the relevant probability space and meaning of greater plausibility are not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling for explanation is warranted, while favoring a creator over multiverse alternatives requires further comparative priors and likelihoods.

charity.alternative: A multiverse or unknown natural account could explain observer-compatible constants without an intelligent selector.
charity.decisiveQualification: Empirical inaccessibility does not by itself make the creator hypothesis more probable, and the creator's own explanatory status remains disputed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible, but it moves from explanatory demand to creator preference without a fully defended comparative probability bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The narrow life-permitting role of constants is specifically described, but representativeness, probability measures, and serious rival comparison remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable creator bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The rival is recognized but dismissed with insufficient attention to the decisive comparative qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Collins describes the precise parameters required for complexity and thought, says they cry out for explanation, and contrasts creator and multiverse accounts.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning may count against creator theism because an unconstrained God should not require life to depend on a narrow physical knife edge or hostile meta-conditions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the fine-tuning question to Alex, whose extended objection continues through an analogy completed in the delivered lookahead context.

components.text: Whether narrow life-permitting constants are more expected under an unconstrained intelligent creator.

response.rationale: O'Connor expressly diagnoses the creator inference's likelihood problem: an omnipotent creator need not make life depend upon hostile knife-edge meta-conditions, so fine-tuning may be unexpected rather than expected on theism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the decisive comparative inference and states the reversal consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The likelihood-reversal challenge and its conditional framing are clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully framed as a possible reversal rather than a conclusive disproof.

charity.alternative: A creator may value orderly, law-governed embodiment and therefore choose parameters that permit such life.
charity.decisiveQualification: That purpose would need to explain why life must remain dependent on a narrow and hostile physical range despite divine power.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reversal coherently challenges the likelihood premise rather than merely offering an unrelated alternative.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual contrast between omnipotence and knife-edge dependence is specific, though no formal likelihood comparison is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con fine-tuning-reversal bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest orderly-creation reply remains available, but the move accurately identifies the qualification it must answer.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor argues that a creator should not need hostile meta-conditions set on a knife edge and uses an alternative-creator analogy to reverse the inference.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: God creates through orderly laws, and God's desire for loving relationships guides the selection of physical parameters capable of producing complex creatures.
moves.attributionBasis: The response adopts Collins's characteristic theistic commitments and directly answers the immediately preceding challenge about divine constraint.

components.text: Why a powerful God would choose narrow physical parameters rather than create life under different conditions.

response.rationale: Collins answers that orderly physical means serve God's relational goal and treats suitable parameters as means to that end, but he does not fully explain why alternative parameters were unavailable.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive purpose question but leaves the omnipotence and alternative-parameters component substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Purpose and orderly means are clear, but the claimed relation between the end and these particular parameters remains underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The proposed purpose makes the parameters compatible with theism but does not establish their comparative probability.

charity.alternative: Omnipotence may permit the same relational end through different constants or laws.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling current parameters a means does not show that this means was necessary or especially expected.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A valued orderly means can explain a choice, but the reply does not bridge from God's end to the necessity or preference for these parameters.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claims about God's identity, goal, and preferred means are asserted rather than independently supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con reversal by offering a purposive explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges the constraint question but omits its decisive modal qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Collins says God's desire to love creatures supplies the end and the physical parameters are orderly means to achieving it.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Physical constants are not logical necessities, so claiming that God could not produce a life-permitting universe under different constants poses a genuine challenge to divine omnipotence.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn is a continuous conceptual objection in O'Connor's voice, contrasting physical impossibility with logical contradiction.

components.text: Whether God's chosen relational end explains or necessitates the specific life-permitting constants.
Whether the constants support an intelligent creator without creating an omnipotence problem.

response.rationale: O'Connor distinguishes logical impossibility from merely different physics and argues that inability to create life with altered gravity would challenge omnipotence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the modal premise left unresolved by Collins and links it to the fine-tuning inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The logical-versus-physical impossibility distinction is sharply and stably stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: O'Connor presents a genuine challenge rather than claiming a decisive contradiction.

charity.alternative: Omnipotence excludes logical contradictions but need not make every stipulated physical package internally coherent.
charity.decisiveQualification: The example changes gravity without identifying any logical contradiction in life existing under the altered law.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The modal distinction is explicit and directly exposes the unsupported move from physical dependence to divine inability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The gravity example concretely supports the conceptual challenge, though its actual biological coherence is not demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central fine-tuning-reversal burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately incorporates the strongest standard limitation on omnipotence and identifies what remains unexplained.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor contrasts impossible square circles with a universe having stronger gravity and argues the latter does not appear logically contradictory.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Immense and apparently unnecessary evolutionary suffering is expected under atheistic naturalism but surprising under a loving creator intending relationship with human beings.
moves.attributionBasis: The long uninterrupted argument is framed explicitly through O'Connor's comparison of expectations under atheism and theism.

response.rationale: Constructively compares the expected scale of animal suffering under naturalism and loving-creator theism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies a direct comparative likelihood argument central to the suffering route, with concrete categories and scale.

precisionFindings.rationale: The apparently unnecessary suffering, competing hypotheses, and expectation claim are clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is expressed as an expectation judgment, not a deductive incompatibility.

charity.alternative: Stable laws and evolution may be valuable lawful means through which a creator produces autonomous embodied life.
charity.decisiveQualification: That account must explain the immense quantity and apparently avoidable severity of nonhuman suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The expected-evidence comparison is validly structured and avoids treating suffering as a strict contradiction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites the enormous present and historical scale of animal suffering, though it does not systematically establish avoidability or compare all theistic goods.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable con suffering-counterevidence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly leaves compatibility open while pressing the decisive comparative quantity problem.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor stresses the unfathomable number of suffering animals and asks whether this is expected if reality was organized for loving relationship with humans.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: Evolution's suffering is compatible with a God of order because an elegant lawful creative process can be providentially directed without repeated supernatural interventions.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly grants the difficulty and responds with Collins's account of natural law, evolution, and providential direction.

components.text: Why a loving creator would employ an evolutionary process containing extensive pain and suffering.

response.rationale: Collins grants the suffering and answers that elegant evolution coheres with a God of order better than repeated supernatural intervention, but does not explain the scale or necessity of agony.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive divine-method question but only partially answers the quantity and avoidability challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The lawful-plan answer is clear, though 'directed' and the relevant degree of intervention remain underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It establishes compatibility more readily than comparative expectation or necessity.

charity.alternative: A loving creator could use stable evolutionary laws while reducing predation, agony, waste, or extinction.
charity.decisiveQualification: Elegance and nonintervention alone do not show that the observed amount of suffering was required.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Lawful evolution coherently explains nonintervention, but compatibility with order does not explain why this much suffering accompanies the process.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evolution's lawfulness is grounded, while providential direction and the superiority of this plan are largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central suffering-counterevidence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move grants pain but does not engage the strongest less-suffering lawful alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Collins calls evolution an elegant, scientifically well-designed process consistent with a God of order and expressly acknowledges its pain and suffering.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Unknown divine reasons for suffering permit an equivalent appeal to unknown natural explanations for fine-tuning, while less agonizing lawful ecosystems show that animal suffering was avoidable.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly compares skeptical replies to suffering and fine-tuning, then develops concrete alternatives to predation-based evolution.

components.text: Whether appeal to an unknown providential lawful plan adequately explains evolutionary suffering.
Whether unexplained fine-tuning can be treated asymmetrically from unexplained divine reasons for suffering.

response.rationale: O'Connor directly challenges the appeal to unknown divine reasons by applying the same restraint to fine-tuning and offers less-agonizing lawful alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both the epistemic symmetry and avoidability components with an explicit counterexample strategy.

precisionFindings.rationale: The symmetry claim and the less-suffering alternative are distinctly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues for symmetrical restraint and avoidability without claiming exhaustive knowledge.

charity.alternative: The theist may possess independent evidence for God that licenses trust in unknown reasons, unlike an unsupported naturalistic unknown.
charity.decisiveQualification: That asymmetry depends on independent evidence strong enough to survive the suffering evidence rather than on the mystery appeal itself.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The symmetry challenge is coherent, and the proposed lawful alternatives directly pressure the claim that suffering comes with any ordered package.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move provides concrete conceptual alternatives, though their ecological feasibility and full consequences are not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly reinforces the central suffering-counterevidence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest asymmetry is available, and the move correctly identifies its dependence on independent support.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor compares unknown divine reasons with unknown fine-tuning explanations and argues that lawful ecosystems need not involve the observed forms of agony.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: Physical suffering follows from stable natural laws, and avoiding it would require continual divine intervention that would compromise God's ordered creation.
moves.attributionBasis: The response acknowledges O'Connor's objection and invokes a physicist-priest's category of physical evil in Collins's own defense.

components.text: Whether apparently avoidable suffering follows from stable laws rather than an arbitrary divine choice.
Why innocent animal and human suffering occurs under a loving ordered creation.

response.rationale: Collins explains earthquakes and related harms as consequences of stable physical laws and says eliminating them would require continuing intervention, but does not show that all relevant laws or harms are necessary.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the stable-law demand with a concrete example while only partially addressing avoidability and comparative expectation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The earthquake example is clear, but the generalization from tectonics to physical suffering as a package is broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Stable laws explain proximate mechanisms, while the stronger claim that avoidance requires continual intervention is insufficiently established.

charity.alternative: A creator could choose different stable laws, initial conditions, or biological pain systems rather than continually suspend current laws.
charity.decisiveQualification: The earthquake example does not eliminate those alternative ordered designs.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Stable laws explain how harms occur, but the move risks conflating explanation of mechanism with justification of the chosen law system.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Plate tectonics supplies a specific example, while the claim that the whole package is unavoidable lacks comparative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central suffering-counterevidence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses intervention under current laws but omits the decisive alternative-law qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Collins cites lethal earthquakes caused by moving tectonic plates and argues that avoiding such consequences would require divine interruption of physical law.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: Historical testimony, the empty tomb, resurrection appearances, and witnesses' costly persistence make Jesus's bodily resurrection the most likely explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer is explicitly introduced as Collins's reason for finding the resurrection historically compelling and continues through his miracle objection response.

response.rationale: Constructively infers bodily resurrection from testimony, the empty tomb, appearances, and witnesses' costly persistence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supplies the principal Christianity-specific historical inference, though source independence and alternatives are compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory conclusion and evidence categories are clear; the comparison class behind 'most likely' remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling resurrection the most likely explanation outruns the selected span's treatment of source dependence, prior probability, and ordinary alternatives.

charity.alternative: Grief experiences, memory development, theological legend, or mixed natural processes could generate the traditions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Costly sincerity would not by itself verify bodily resurrection, and the sources require independence and dating analysis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidence can support sincere resurrection belief, but the bridge to bodily resurrection as most likely requires defended source and comparative assumptions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several historical considerations are named, yet their independence, reliability, martyrdom basis, and alternative explanations are not seriously established here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable Christian-specificity bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The inference compresses decisive rival and source-critical qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Collins invokes the empty tomb, appearances, testimony, and persistent costly witness, then identifies actual resurrection as the most likely explanation.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Resurrection appearances are better explained as legendary development because the earliest form of Mark lacks them and later sources supply increasingly elaborate accounts.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor introduces the historical question and traces the resurrection traditions through successive Gospel sources.

components.text: Whether resurrection appearances and witness traditions are historically reliable enough to make bodily resurrection most likely.

response.rationale: O'Connor directly supplies a source-development alternative, contrasting Mark's earliest ending with later, more elaborate appearance narratives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the reliability and rival-explanation demand, although it does not address every item such as Pauline testimony.

precisionFindings.rationale: The chronological-development claim is clear, though 'fanciful' compresses several distinct literary changes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Later elaboration supports development, but absence of appearances from Mark's extant ending does not alone establish that all appearance traditions are legendary.

charity.alternative: Paul's earlier testimony and independent traditions may precede Mark and preserve resurrection appearances.
charity.decisiveQualification: Gospel elaboration does not by itself resolve the antiquity or independence of Pauline and pre-Gospel material.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Increasing elaboration can support legendary development, but the inference is incomplete without incorporating earlier Pauline evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Mark-to-later-Gospels comparison is specific and relevant, though source relationships and earlier traditions are not fully assessed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con Christian-evidence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move gives a serious source-critical rival but omits a decisive earlier-source qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor states that earliest Mark lacks post-resurrection appearances and that later Gospels increase witnesses and narrative elaboration.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: Cross-cultural recognition of good and evil points beyond evolutionary explanation toward a holy source of goodness and love.
moves.attributionBasis: Collins explicitly restates O'Connor's earlier objection before presenting his own cross-cultural moral distinction and inference.

components.text: Whether moral experience supports a transcendent good despite moral objections to Christian texts.
Whether features of moral experience supply affirmative evidence beyond skeptical mystery.

response.rationale: Collins argues that cross-cultural moral recognition exceeds his sociobiological explanation and points to a holy source, but he does not answer the biblical slavery and women objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the general evidential status of morality but leaves the opponent's decisive internal Christian moral conflict uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The transcendent-source inference is clear, but the claimed cross-cultural scope and what evolution cannot explain remain broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Personal explanatory failure makes transcendence possible but does not establish a holy loving source as the best explanation.

charity.alternative: Evolutionary and cultural processes may explain shared moral dispositions without exhausting normative moral truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not distinguish genetic, cultural, and philosophical explanations or show why a personal holy source follows.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move passes from limits of a sociobiological account to a holy loving source through multiple underdefended bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Cross-cultural moral recognition is asserted, and no representative data or serious evolutionary-cultural comparison is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports morality's role in the central cumulative-force bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The naturalistic alternative is mentioned but materially compressed at its decisive explanatory points.

moves.evidenceBasis: Collins says sociobiology did not explain perceived moral obligation and infers an extra-scientific holy source concerned with goodness and love.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: The New Testament's sweeping portrayal of Jesus and its resurrection case can rationally compel commitment without resolving every textual dispute or attaining proof.
moves.attributionBasis: Collins speaks in the first person about his approach to the New Testament, Jesus's teaching, and the resurrection literature.

components.text: Whether source-critical disputes defeat rational reliance on the New Testament's resurrection portrayal.
Whether the holistic portrayal of Jesus overcomes specific moral objections to Christianity.

response.rationale: Collins directly says the sweeping New Testament portrayal remains compelling despite M, Q, addition, and subtraction disputes, but offers personal holistic resonance rather than resolving the source-development inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It recognizes the decisive source-critical issue but only partially answers it and does not contact the distinct moral objection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The holistic method is recoverable, but 'ringing true' and 'sweeping terms' provide unstable evidential criteria.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Personal compulsion is appropriately qualified, but it supplies limited public warrant against the historical objection.

charity.alternative: Later theological coherence and personal resonance can coexist with legendary development or textual unreliability.
charity.decisiveQualification: A holistic impression does not answer the chronology, independence, and elaboration of resurrection sources.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Holistic trust can coexist with unresolved details, but it does not logically defeat the specific legendary-development inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The support rests heavily on personal resonance and general reading rather than source-critical comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con Christian-evidence bridge, albeit weakly.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges scholarly disputes but bypasses their decisive historical implications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Collins acknowledges M, Q, additions, and subtractions but says the New Testament's broad account of God, Jesus, crucifixion, and resurrection rings true and compels him.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Personal revelation could raise an individual's belief in God, but private experience has little force as public evidence and intellectual argument cannot be the only accessible route to faith.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn begins with O'Connor's conditional response to Collins's experience and develops his view of private versus public justification.

components.text: Whether personally compelling Christian revelation supplies adequate public warrant for commitment.
Whether noncoercive evidence can rationally differ between personal and public contexts.
Whether public historical arguments independently establish Christianity.

response.rationale: O'Connor grants that personal revelation may legitimately raise individual belief while explaining why it carries little public force, thereby directly distinguishing private justification from debate evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully contacts the private-versus-public warrant issue but does not answer the independent historical case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between personal and public evidential force is clear and carefully limited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move expressly allows personal revelation to be legitimate while limiting interpersonal force.

charity.alternative: Private revelation may rationally combine with public evidence in an individual's cumulative case.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its inability to transfer directly does not show it has no individual evidential force, a point O'Connor expressly grants.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The personal/public justification distinction is explicit, consistent, and avoids denying what the argument only limits.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is primarily epistemic and well illustrated by public-debate conditions, though broader testimony theory is not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con Christian-evidence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately preserves the strongest individual-justification qualification while limiting public use.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor calls personal revelation potentially legitimate for the experiencer but says it will not ordinarily convince another person in public debate.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
moves.proposition: Experiences of numinous beauty and musical longing can provide fleeting indications of a transcendent reality that ordinary natural description may miss.
moves.attributionBasis: Collins identifies his earlier atheistic perspective, supplies a detailed musical example, and then asks O'Connor about comparable experiences.

response.rationale: Constructively offers intense, fleeting musical longing as experiential evidence suggestive of transcendence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies a distinct cumulative consideration with a vivid example, while leaving the inference beyond natural description compressed.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The diversity of objects and experiences called beautiful makes it difficult to infer a single intrinsic maximum of beauty resembling God.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning, suffering, beauty, and the resurrection remain profound mysteries that do not justify confident conclusions about God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor synthesizes the debate's principal subjects in a continuous first-person statement of his skeptical epistemic position.

components.text: Whether the combined mysteries justify trust rather than continued agnostic restraint.
Whether fine-tuning supports a confident creator inference.
Whether resurrection evidence supports a confident Christian conclusion.
Whether beauty licenses confident metaphysical conclusions.

response.rationale: O'Connor synthesizes fine-tuning, resurrection, suffering, and beauty as unresolved high-consequence questions and argues that their combination warrants caution rather than confidence.
